what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Twenty-five openable vaults are hidden from the homepage
sections.para: The most persuasive thing on sgit.ai is twenty-five real vaults a stranger can open in one click, up from four three weeks ago, yet the homepage shows none. It leads with invisible encryption and buries the artefacts in a table. This diagnosis, with screenshots, comes before the rebuild so the two can be compared.

sections.label: The homepage leads with the thing you cannot see
sections.line: The homepage leads with encryption, which nobody can see
sections.para: Every word of the first screen is true but unpersuasive, because encryption and zero knowledge cannot be looked at. Visitors take the value on faith, then see a familiar git-style terminal walkthrough that shows familiarity, not power. The word vault appears three times in the hero, and no vault is shown.

sections.label: The use cases are abstract while twenty-five concrete ones sit one level down
sections.line: Abstract use cases hide twenty-five concrete examples below
sections.para: The use-case band lists categories, such as multi-agent collaboration on branches, which describe capabilities rather than show them. One level down sits a vault where one agent copied another's catalogue byte for byte and added a conformance layer, with passing tests. The homepage has the abstraction; the proof is elsewhere.

sections.label: The proof is a table, two clicks away
sections.line: A good table finds vaults but does not convince
sections.para: The vaults sit behind a dropdown, in a table rebuilt this week: sortable, categorised, newest first, with read keys moved off. A table suits a visitor who already wants a vault, not one deciding. Visitors could instead open a vault in one click, running in the browser with its data, sources and tests.

sections.label: The strongest story has no front door
sections.line: The agents-building-for-agents story has no front door
sections.para: The site's strongest story is one person and agents building for each other: a brief published 6 September became a vault the same day, was corrected by the API team, and a fork kept a fourteen-version history labelling seven reconstructed. It is filed under Docs as a log, not told end to end.

sections.label: One gap worth naming
sections.line: No vault demonstrates the branch-per-agent merge claim
sections.para: The homepage promises a branch per agent with a human reviewing the merge, but every published vault was built by one agent or on another's finished work. None shows two agents' branches and a human merge. Publishing such a vault, or running the next build to show it, is the highest-value addition.

sections.label: The fix, in order
sections.line: Reorder so proof comes before mechanism, and cut
sections.para: The homepage has nine bands and 1,370 words. The fix: a hero with four real vault cards, pip install second, six vaults chosen by job and generated from the table's data, the one-human-many-agents story with its own page, then the terminal and zero-knowledge explanation. The three doors band moves to docs.

sections.label: And a page that says who is behind it
sections.line: A page will say who is behind the site
sections.para: A beta tool asking people to publish read keys needs a page saying who is asking. It will cover who builds sgit, agents included, why, and the commercial line, borrowing Interests declared and Reach me, or correct me from open-source.sgit.ai. A new network card shows each sibling site's own description.

sections.label: What happens next
sections.line: The rebuild is next, then an honest before-and-after
sections.para: The rebuild comes in the next release. The following article will set the new homepage beside these screenshots and say what changed and what it cost, including if the before pictures still look better. Written by Dinis Cruz and his agentic team, licensed CC BY 4.0.
